05 Behavioral (RT, eye tracking) and physiological measures (ECG, EEG)
10/49
Main lesson: Physiological data are NOT objective. They are undifferentiated effects of the body 
with multiple potential causes. Hypothesize the cause, then predict the effect (not reversely). Use 
triangulation to make sense of observations 
Measuring muscle temperature will not help 
the researcher with the interpretation of 
facial expressions
In 90% of real-life cases, people smile out of 
frustration. Huge problem for any sentiment-
analysis system (Hoque & Picard, 2011)

Main lesson: Bayes is an alternative (or complement) to frequentism. It does not say yes or no to a 
hypothesis, it merely indicates a degree of confidence in the result
My machine is similar to a...
H1: human being
H2: an animal
H3: a plant
For instance,
P(H1) = 50%, P(H2) = 10%, P(H3) = 40%
In Bayes, this is your prior knowledge, the knowledge you start from

Yes, Johan Hoorn’s ACASIA model of creativity is a well-known framework in the field of 
creativity research. The ACASIA model stands for “Associative, Combinatorial, Analogical, 
Situational, Intentional and Adaptive” and it proposes that creativity arises from the 
interaction between these six dimensions.
According to Hoorn’s model, associative thinking involves making connections between 
seemingly unrelated ideas or concepts; combinatorial thinking involves combining existing 
ideas or concepts in new ways; analogical thinking involves drawing parallels between 
different domains or contexts; situational thinking involves considering the context in 
which a problem or idea arises; intentional thinking involves setting goals and directing 
attention towards specific outcomes; and adaptive thinking involves being flexible and 
open to change.
Hoorn argues that all six dimensions are necessary for creative thought to occur. His 
model has been used by researchers to study various aspects of creativity such as 
problem-solving, innovation, and artistic expression.

Abstract
In this study, I explored the impact of Generative AI on learning efficacy in academic reading 
materials using experimental methods. College-educated participants engaged in three cycles of 
reading and writing tasks. After each cycle, they responded to comprehension questions related 
to the material. After adjusting for background knowledge and demographic factors, complete 
reliance on AI for writing tasks led to a 25.1% reduction in accuracy. In contrast, AI-assisted 
reading resulted in a 12% decline. Interestingly, using AI for summarization significantly 
improved both quality and output. Accuracy exhibited notable variance in the AI-assisted 
section. Further analysis revealed that individuals with a robust background in the reading 
topic and superior reading/writing skills benefitted the most. I conclude the research by 
discussing educational policy implications, emphasizing the need for educators to warn students 
about the dangers of over-dependence on AI and provide guidance on its optimal use in 
educational settings.
Ju, Q. (2023). Experimental Evidence on Negative Impact of Generative AI on Scientific Learning Outcomes. arXiv preprint arXiv:2311.05629.
What do you think: Teachers (robust background, superior skills) can but students cannot use AI?

ummary
Main lessons:
No matter the scientific approach, all observation boils 
down to signal detection
A precise RQ guides you through the entire research 
process, because you will be distracted by the many 
details you encounter and biases you have
Qualitative methods are for idea formation and later 
can be (should be) quantified. Qualitative methods do 
not ‘test’ anything
Asking questions is not as easy as it seems. You need 
multiple words for each construct because you do not 
know whether people interpret a word the way you 
intended
Physiological data are NOT objective. They are 
undifferentiated effects of the body with multiple 
potential causes. Hypothesize the cause, then predict 
the effect (not reversely). Use triangulation to make 
sense of observations

pages.text:
ummary
Main lessons:
Correlation is not causation no matter how Big the 
Data are (actually, with more data, significant but 
meaningless correlations are likelier to occur)
Regression techniques tell you which variable is 
responsible for (explains) an observed effect and to 
what degree. There will always be variance 
unexplained – those are the things we did not keep 
under control or the things we have no theory about
Hypothesis testing is very precise at the cost of 
answering but limited aspects of a theory. Therefore, 
do experiments on the crucial assumptions – those 
that make theories crumble and fall
Frequentism is but one view on the data. It cannot do 
more than rejecting ‘no difference’ or fail to do so. It 
cannot confirm ‘there is an effect’
Bayes is an alternative (or complement) to 
frequentism. It does not say yes or no to a hypothesis, 
it merely indicates a degree of confidence in the result
